lesson_title: Count the Teeth, Get the Number
hook_text: Your toy motor lifts 20 grams. Your cage weighs 300. Here is how gears close that gap, with arithmetic you already know.
clip_script: Mechanical advantage of a gear pair: driven teeth over driver teeth. 60 over 15 is 4: four times the force, a quarter of the speed. Diameters give the same answer. One pair rarely beats 5, and you need 15, plus a margin, call it 25. So stack stages: fix two gears on one shaft, big one driven, small one driving the next, and the ratios multiply. 60 over 12 twice is 25. Now check speed: 3 000 rpm over 25 is 120 at the drum, which on a 40 millimetre drum shoots the cage up at 15 metres a minute. Too fast. Go to 60 to 1, or shrink the drum, which also helps the force. Count the meshes for direction; fix it with an idler. Then write the train down as a list. That list is your winder specification, and the tender board will ask for it.
visual_style: Spring balance and toy motor on a whiteboard bench; 60/15 = 4 appears; gears stack on shared shafts with x4, x4, x4 multiplying to 64; a drum shrinks and the cage slows; a list of stages writes itself.
pacing: The ratio, why stages, the multiplication, the speed check, the specification.
call_to_action: Watch the full lesson and work out the ratio your team's kit can reach with two stages.
